title: PhD: LLM-Based Distributed Autonomy (AIDA)
summary: Research how small language models can plan and coordinate autonomous vehicles in real time.
tasks: Run compact language models for real-time reasoning on the vehicle.
Design a shared fleet memory that keeps only unusual or safety-relevant episodes.
Study distributed planning with limited communication, including safe fallbacks.
Evaluate in simulation and on our RoboRacer cars.
background: Master’s degree or equivalent in a relevant field.
Strong background in control, machine learning, autonomous systems or related methods.
subject: PhD enquiry: LLM-Based Distributed Autonomy (AIDA)

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: AIDA (AI-Driven Distributed Autonomy, FWF) studies how small language models can support planning and coordination in safety-critical driving. Vehicles keep only unusual or safety-relevant episodes in a shared fleet memory and recall similar cases in unfamiliar situations. Evaluation uses simulation and our RoboRacer cars, possibly extending to full-scale vehicles. The position runs 30 months at 40 h/week; start to be confirmed. To apply, send a CV, a one-page motivation letter, transcripts and two academic referees to joinus@trustcps.eu.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Supervisor: Ezio Bartocci. Co-supervisor: Agnes Poks (Project PI, TU Wien).

title: 3D Raceline Optimization with Banking and Elevation
summary: Extend our 2D raceline optimizer to tracks with elevation and banking.
tasks: Review and document the current raceline code with its original developer.
Build a 3D track model with elevation, banking and curvature.
Add gravity and geometry-dependent acceleration limits to the optimization.
Compare the result with our 2D optimizer and TUM’s 3D raceline tool.
Test on non-planar track sections in simulation and, if practical, on our race car.
background: Mechanical engineering, control, robotics or computational engineering background.
Vehicle dynamics, optimal control and numerical optimization.
Python, MATLAB, CasADi or C++. Differential geometry helps but is not required.
subject: Project enquiry: 3D Raceline Optimization with Banking and Elevation

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Our raceline tool treats the track as flat, so it ignores elevation, banking and off-camber turns. These change gravity and normal load, and with them the best path and speed profile. With a 3D LiDAR map we can describe the track as a 3D road. The outcome is a documented 3D version of the optimizer and a clear answer to when 3D geometry changes the path, speed or lap time. Testing needs a track section with elevation or banking.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Philipp Gratzer, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: 3D LiDAR–Inertial Mapping of Race Tracks
summary: Build accurate, repeatable 3D maps of our race tracks from LiDAR and IMU data.
tasks: Calibrate LiDAR and IMU and set up a repeatable data recording.
Benchmark existing mapping systems such as LIO-SAM, FAST-LIO2 and GLIM.
Find where they fail: motion distortion, vibration, few features, repeated geometry.
Implement one targeted improvement for racing conditions.
Evaluate map accuracy, repeatability, runtime and usefulness for raceline optimization.
background: Robotics, computer vision, geomatics or computational engineering background.
3D geometry, coordinate transforms and probabilistic estimation.
C++/ROS or Python. Experience with point clouds or LiDAR odometry is a plus.
subject: Project enquiry: 3D LiDAR–Inertial Mapping of Race Tracks

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: A 3D LiDAR lets the car capture elevation, banking and barriers that our 2D map cannot hold. Such maps feed 3D localization, raceline optimization and perception. Existing mapping tools are a good start, but racing brings fast rotations, vibration, limited onboard compute and repetitive track sections. The outcome is a reproducible mapping pipeline, consistent maps with a road-surface model, and a comparison of existing tools plus one improvement. Localizing in the finished map is a separate thesis.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: Sideslip Estimation with Optical Flow Sensors
summary: Estimate the car’s sideslip with downward-facing optical flow sensors and use it in our MPC.
tasks: Mount and calibrate the optical flow sensors under the car.
Model the measurements, correcting for rotation and changes in pitch and roll.
Fuse optical flow with IMU, wheel speed and steering in an EKF, UKF or MHE.
Check the estimates against motion capture or another ground truth.
Feed the estimate into the MPC and refine the raceline limits.
background: Mechanical engineering, control, mechatronics or signal processing background.
Vehicle dynamics and state estimation.
Python, MATLAB, embedded programming or ROS, and interest in hands-on sensor work.
subject: Project enquiry: Sideslip Estimation with Optical Flow Sensors

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Sideslip angle shows how close the car is to the grip limit, but our standard sensors cannot measure it. Model-based estimates get worse when tires or surface change, which is exactly when sideslip matters most. Downward optical flow sensors measure ground motion directly but are affected by height, attitude, texture and vibration. The outcome is a calibrated sensor setup, an estimator with known accuracy and failure cases, and a test of whether sideslip feedback helps near the limit.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: Nonlinear MPC on the GPU
summary: Move our racing MPC to a GPU solver and find out where parallel computation actually helps.
tasks: Benchmark the current CPU-based MPC as a baseline.
Implement the racing MPC in TurboMPC or a similar GPU framework.
Try one or two GPU strategies, such as batched multi-start optimization.
Find when the GPU beats the CPU for different horizons, models and batch sizes.
Test the controller in simulation and on our race car.
background: Control, robotics, computational engineering or a related background.
Optimization and vehicle dynamics. Python, JAX, CUDA or C++ helps.
Interest in numerical algorithms. GPU programming experience is a plus, not a must.
subject: Project enquiry: Nonlinear MPC on the GPU

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Nonlinear MPC can use the tire limits better than simpler controllers, but its compute cost limits horizon length, model detail and replanning rate. GPU solvers like TurboMPC solve many problems in parallel and have been used in full-scale racing. We want to know where this pays off on a small car with limited compute, looking at solver latency, CPU–GPU transfer, power use and lap performance. The outcome is a working GPU MPC and a clear comparison with the CPU version.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: Real-Time RGB-D Obstacle Detection and Tracking
summary: Build a fast obstacle detector and tracker that combines color and depth images on the car.
tasks: Define which obstacles to detect and record a labeled RGB-D test set.
Calibrate and sync the color and depth streams, and study depth errors while driving.
Implement fast depth-based detection, for example ground removal and clustering.
Compare RGB-only, depth-only and fused approaches.
Add tracking, run the best pipeline onboard and test it in closed loop.
background: Computer vision, robotics, embedded systems or computational engineering background.
Camera geometry, image processing and machine learning.
Python, C++/ROS or PyTorch. ONNX or TensorRT is a plus.
subject: Thesis enquiry: Real-Time RGB-D Obstacle Detection and Tracking

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Our current detector is simple and works in controlled demos but can fail when obstacles look different, depth is noisy or the car moves fast. Missed obstacles are dangerous; false alarms slow the car needlessly. Color helps recognize objects and depth helps separate them from the ground. For racing, latency and stable tracking matter as much as per-frame accuracy. The outcome is a pipeline that runs on our race car within a fixed latency budget, plus a labeled test set.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: Localization That Recovers from Failures
summary: Improve our car’s localization so it notices its own errors and recovers from them.
tasks: Find where the current particle filter and EKF fail, e.g. under wheel slip or dropouts.
Compare alternatives: an improved particle filter, a fixed-lag smoother or a factor graph.
Add checks that keep unreliable measurements out of the estimate.
Add global relocalization with place recognition, possibly using ideas from BioSLAM.
Evaluate accuracy, recovery time and lap performance in simulation and on our race car.
background: Robotics, mechatronics, control or computational engineering background.
Probabilistic estimation, coordinate transforms and sensor fusion.
Python or C++/ROS. Particle filters, Kalman filters or factor graphs are a plus.
subject: Thesis enquiry: Localization That Recovers from Failures

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Small pose errors become large tracking errors at racing speed. Our car uses a particle filter with an EKF. It works, but wheel slip, hard acceleration, repetitive track sections, sensor dropouts or a wrong initial pose can make it confidently wrong. The goal is localization that stays accurate during normal racing and recovers when it fails. It stays with 2D map-based localization and current sensors. The outcome includes a comparison showing when to keep, improve or extend the particle filter.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: Online Vehicle Parameter Estimation While Racing
summary: Estimate changing tire, steering and drivetrain parameters while driving and feed them to the MPC.
tasks: Pick a few parameters that can really be identified, e.g. tire stiffness or actuator delay.
Design safe test maneuvers and an offline reference identification.
Implement a recursive estimator with uncertainty, parameter bounds and update checks.
Send fast updates to the MPC and slower ones to the raceline optimizer.
Test in simulation and on our race car under changing conditions.
background: Control, mechanical engineering, mechatronics or computational engineering background.
Vehicle dynamics, parameter estimation and system identification.
Python or MATLAB. Recursive estimation, optimization or MPC is a plus.
subject: Thesis enquiry: Online Vehicle Parameter Estimation While Racing

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Our raceline optimizer and MPC need an accurate vehicle model, but we identify its parameters once before racing. Tire wear and temperature, friction, battery voltage, payload or hardware changes make it drift. Estimating too many coupled parameters gives unstable models, so this thesis keeps the set small and keeps updates from destabilizing the controller. The outcome is an online identification pipeline, an answer to which parameters can be tracked during racing, and an improvement under at least one changing condition.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: 3D LiDAR Map Localization with Global Recovery
summary: Localize the car in a prebuilt 3D track map in real time and recover when tracking is lost.
tasks: Set up a fixed 3D reference map, calibration and ground-truth evaluation.
Implement a fast LiDAR–inertial scan-to-map localization baseline.
Estimate when the scan alignment can be trusted and when it cannot.
Add global relocalization and define when to switch between tracking and recovery.
Evaluate accuracy, recovery success and time, runtime and lap performance on our race car.
background: Robotics, computer vision, control or computational engineering background.
3D geometry, state estimation and point cloud registration.
C++/ROS preferred. Factor graphs, LiDAR odometry or global registration are a plus.
subject: Thesis enquiry: 3D LiDAR Map Localization with Global Recovery

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Once we have a 3D map, the car must localize in it quickly enough for racing control. Scan-to-map alignment gives precise 6-DoF poses but can fail on repetitive geometry, during hard manoeuvres or with a bad initial pose. The system should notice when its alignment is wrong, never silently accept a bad match, and recover globally. The map is fixed; building it is a separate thesis. The outcome is a real-time localization pipeline with confidence indicators and tested recovery.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: Adapting Liquid Neural Network Vehicle Models to New Conditions
summary: Adapt a physics-plus-Liquid vehicle model to new tires, friction or payload with little new data.
tasks: Start from our hybrid physics and Liquid model and pick one change, e.g. friction.
Record a small dataset under the new condition.
Compare updating the physical parameters, fine-tuning the Liquid residual, or both.
Measure prediction error, physical consistency and how much data is needed.
Test the best model with an existing predictive controller on our race car.
background: Mechanical or computational engineering background, with Python or MATLAB.
Physical modeling and parameter estimation. Basic neural network fine-tuning helps; no Liquid network experience needed.
Interest in hands-on experiments with our race cars.
subject: Thesis enquiry: Adapting Liquid Neural Network Vehicle Models to New Conditions

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: A vehicle model tuned for one setup loses accuracy when tires, friction, payload or the car itself change. Retraining from scratch ignores that most of the physics stays the same and needs a lot of data. We start from a physical model with a pretrained LRC/LrcSSM residual, introduce one change on our race car, and ask which part to adapt. The outcome is a reproducible transfer workflow and a clear answer: update the physics, the Liquid residual, or both.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Monika Farsang and Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: Physics-Informed Liquid Neural Networks for Vehicle Dynamics
summary: Combine a physical vehicle model with a Liquid neural network residual and use it in MPC.
tasks: Set up a lateral/yaw single-track model with a suitable tire model.
Identify its parameters from new or existing driving data of our race car.
Train an MLP and a Liquid residual (LRC or LrcSSM) on the remaining model error.
Compare physical, learned and hybrid models on accuracy, plausibility, data needs and runtime.
Use the best model in our MPC/MPCC and test it in simulation and on the car.
background: Mechanical or computational engineering background.
Physical modeling and parameter estimation; Python or MATLAB.
Basic neural network fine-tuning helps. No Liquid network experience needed.
subject: Thesis enquiry: Physics-Informed Liquid Neural Networks for Vehicle Dynamics

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Single-track models are interpretable but miss tire and actuator effects near the limit. Data-driven models capture these but need more data and generalize poorly. Here the physical model does most of the work and a compact Liquid neural network learns only what is left. The thesis covers lateral/yaw dynamics on our race car, tested open-loop and inside an existing MPC/MPCC. The outcome is an interpretable hybrid model that predicts better than the physical baseline and still runs in real time.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Monika Farsang, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: Diffusion Models as Overtaking Priors for MPCC
summary: Train a diffusion model to propose overtaking trajectories that an MPCC controller then refines and executes.
tasks: Generate simulated racing trajectories labeled follow, setup, overtake (left/right) or abort.
Train a conditional diffusion model that proposes short trajectories for each manoeuvre.
Use the proposals as warm starts or references for MPCC.
Find how many samples fit the real-time budget on our race car.
Compare against MPCC without diffusion, and test on the car at low speed if feasible.
background: Interest in generative models and model predictive control.
Experience with machine learning or optimization-based control is a plus.
subject: Thesis enquiry: Diffusion Models as Overtaking Priors for MPCC

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Overtaking has no single right answer: stay behind, attack inside, go around the outside, wait for the next straight, or abort. Diffusion models can learn such multimodal choices from data. Here the diffusion model does not steer the car. It suggests manoeuvre candidates, and MPCC still handles dynamics, track limits and collision avoidance. The outcome is a prototype with a trajectory dataset, a trained model and MPCC integration, showing whether these priors improve overtaking success or controller convergence.

sections.heading: Supervision
paragraphs: Dr. Agnes Poks, Larisa Clement, Univ. Prof. Ezio Bartocci

title: Learning Safe Overtaking Rules (Neuro-Symbolic)
summary: Learn interpretable overtaking rules that decide when to follow, attack or abort.
tasks: Define racing predicates in Frenet coordinates, such as free gap and time-to-collision.
Train a neural network to estimate these predicates from recent states and track data.
Combine them with differentiable logic (e.g. Logic Tensor Networks) into manoeuvre decisions.
Connect the decisions to MPCC by adjusting its targets and costs.
Compare with rule-based and black-box approaches in simulation, and on the car if feasible.
background: Good Python skills.
PyTorch, sequence models, reinforcement learning or MPC is a plus.
Formal logic helps but is not required.
subject: Thesis enquiry: Learning Safe Overtaking Rules (Neuro-Symbolic)

sections.heading: About
paragraphs: Neural policies can learn overtaking but are hard to interpret and check. Here neural networks estimate simple predicates like “gap on the left is free”, and a differentiable logic layer turns them into manoeuvres such as follow, set up, overtake or abort. The rules start as priors and are tuned from data. MPCC still handles dynamics and safety constraints. The outcome is an interpretable decision layer and an analysis of which rules matter most for safe overtaking.
